skill.name: benchmark-kernel
skill.description: Guides reproducible FlashInfer GPU kernel benchmarks using CUPTI or CUDA events, backend comparisons, correctness checks, and CSV reporting.
skill.summary: Benchmark FlashInfer kernels accurately and compare GPU backends with reproducible settings.
skill.author: flashinfer-ai

security_audit.summary: The 84 Ruby or shell findings are false positives caused by Markdown code formatting. The network finding is a matrix-size argument, not reconnaissance. The optional sudo nvidia-smi command is a confirmed privileged system change requiring explicit approval.

remediation.issue: The troubleshooting guide recommends a privileged GPU clock command.
remediation.suggestion: Mark the command as optional, require explicit confirmation before use, and document how users can restore normal clock management.

content.value_statement: GPU kernel comparisons can be misleading when timing methods and inputs differ. This skill provides reproducible FlashInfer benchmarks with correctness checks and clear performance metrics.
actual_capabilities: Explains when to use CUPTI timing and when CUDA event fallback is acceptable.
Provides benchmark configurations for attention, GEMM, and mixture-of-experts routines.
Shows how to compare supported FlashInfer backends with identical input shapes and data types.
Guides correctness checks, warmup settings, iteration counts, and reproducible command generation.
Explains benchmark metrics and CSV output for later performance analysis.
limitations: Requires a compatible NVIDIA GPU, CUDA installation, FlashInfer checkout, and benchmark dependencies.
CUPTI timing requires CUDA 13 or later and a compatible cupti-python package.
Backend availability depends on GPU compute capability and the selected FlashInfer routine.
The guide does not automate environment setup or validate benchmark results independently.

use_cases.title: Compare attention backends
use_cases.description: Configure identical attention workloads and compare latency, throughput, and consistency across available backends.

use_cases.title: Validate kernel changes
use_cases.description: Run reference checks and reproducible benchmarks before and after a kernel implementation change.

use_cases.title: Build performance reports
use_cases.description: Collect batch benchmark results in CSV format for regression tracking and hardware comparisons.

prompt_templates.title: Create a basic benchmark
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me benchmark a FlashInfer kernel. Ask for my GPU, routine, input shapes, data types, and candidate backends before proposing settings.
prompt_templates.scenario: A beginner needs a valid first benchmark configuration.

prompt_templates.title: Compare selected backends
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a fair backend comparison for [routine] on [GPU]. Use identical inputs, reference checking, warmups, repeated measurements, and reproducible result reporting.
prompt_templates.scenario: A user wants a controlled performance comparison.

prompt_templates.title: Diagnose unstable timing
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these FlashInfer benchmark results: [results]. Identify likely causes of variance and recommend focused changes to warmups, iterations, timing, or cache behavior.
prompt_templates.scenario: A benchmark has high variance or inconsistent measurements.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a regression suite
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a FlashInfer kernel regression plan for [hardware and routines]. Define representative cases, correctness gates, timing controls, CSV fields, and comparison criteria.
prompt_templates.scenario: An advanced team needs repeatable performance monitoring.

output_examples.input: Compare decode attention backends for an H100 with a batch size of 32 and sequence length of 2048.
output: Recommended timing: CUPTI when available, with CUDA events as the documented fallback.
Comparison controls: identical shapes, data types, warmups, iterations, and reference checking.
Report: median latency, standard deviation, throughput, bandwidth, and a reproducible configuration.

output_examples.input: My FP8 GEMM results vary between runs. Suggest a troubleshooting sequence.
output: Increase warmup and measurement iterations before changing the workload.
Confirm the same timing method, clock state, input shapes, and backend list across runs.
Inspect verbose output and compare standard deviation before accepting a performance difference.

output_examples.input: Plan a batch benchmark report for attention, GEMM, and mixture-of-experts kernels.
output_examples.output: The report groups representative workloads by routine, records correctness status, captures timing metrics, and preserves each benchmark configuration for reproduction.

best_practices: Keep shapes, data types, timing methods, and iteration counts identical when comparing backends.
Enable reference checking before treating faster results as valid.
Record GPU details, software versions, benchmark settings, and reproducer information with every result.
anti_patterns: Do not compare results collected with different timing methods without clearly labeling the difference.
Do not disable correctness checks merely to preserve a faster result.
Do not run privileged clock commands on shared hardware without authorization and a restoration plan.

faq.question: Is CUPTI required?
faq.answer: No. The benchmark can use CUDA events, but CUPTI provides more precise hardware-level kernel timing when available.

faq.question: Which routines are covered?
faq.answer: The guide covers FlashInfer attention, GEMM, and mixture-of-experts benchmark routines with representative configurations.

faq.question: Can I compare multiple backends?
faq.answer: Yes. Use identical inputs and enable reference checking so performance differences remain meaningful.

faq.question: Why are my results inconsistent?
faq.answer: Insufficient warmup, few measurements, changing clocks, cache effects, or mixed timing methods can increase variance.

faq.question: Does the skill execute benchmarks automatically?
faq.answer: No. It provides instructions and configurations that users run in a prepared FlashInfer environment.

faq.question: Does GPU clock locking require special care?
faq.answer: Yes. The documented clock command uses sudo, changes system state, and should only run with authorization.
